Failure to thrive (weight/height/head circumference crossing percentiles downward) is a classic red flag for chronic systemic illness (e.g., cardiac, renal, metabolic, or malignancy) and can manifest behaviorally as irritability in toddlers. Since growth data is routinely recorded at well-child visits and often available in records, asking for current weight, height, and head circumference — *and* comparing them to prior measurements — provides objective insight into whether an underlying chronic process is affecting development.

UTIs are notoriously under-recognized in toddlers — up to 50% present *only* with nonspecific signs like irritability, poor feeding, or lethargy, without fever or urinary symptoms. While not yet verified, it is far more common than intracranial pathology or occult infection in this context — especially given absence of fever, vomiting, weight loss, neurologic signs, or lab abnormalities (which would have been flagged if present). Per Rome IV criteria and AAP guidelines, functional GI disorders are the leading cause of chronic irritability in toddlers without systemic signs. Since empiric management is safe and diagnostic (response to laxatives confirms), and no higher-risk diagnosis has been substantiated, this is the most appropriate final diagnosis.
